newsitem.title: UK: Spreads, Copper Week hold focus in metals market.
newsitem.headline: Spreads, Copper Week hold focus in metals market.

text.p: Persistent tightness in copper should keep the industrial metals market alert this week, but activity may ebb lower as players descend on New York for Copper Week.
Medium-term spreads have remained wide, catching off balance a market which had been expecting them to deflate gradually as nearby tight dates mature.
The premium of cash over three months metal dipped as forecast early last week, easing to $145/55 compared to a peak of $335 the previous week.
Later in the week, however, the spread flared unexpectedly above $200, and it was hovering just under there at $185/$195 on Monday morning.
"It would appear that there has been some rolling forward of positions," said analyst Robin Bahr of broker Brandeis.
The market had been expecting tightness to ease after the February prompt next week, but the premium of February over three months nearly tripled last week, Bahr noted.
The spread ended at a $102/12 backwardation by Friday's close from a low of $35/$40 earlier in the week.
A new lump in the structure is said to be forming further down the line.

"People are talking about end of March and early April," Bahr said. Three months before those dates did not see substantial selling, so any tightness would be from players pushing positions forward, he added.
But business may be low-key this week as producers, consumers and traders gather in New York for Copper Week.
On the charts, focus will be on whether three months copper will try lower towards $2,200 after ending weaker on Friday's kerb as a bearish outside day at $2,239.
Above the market, resistance is pegged at $2,280, $2,292 and the November 1996 high of $2,313. To break out of its long-term downtrend, copper would have to surmount $2,320/50, Bahr said.
Zinc and nickel, on the other hand, are looking strong on the charts after having recently breached their long-term bearish trends, he added.
Both markets are looking overbought, but further steam from investment funds could overwhelm the indicators and extend the gains, analysts said.
Important upside targets are $1,239 on zinc, the high from January 1995, and a band from $8,000 to $8,250 for nickel.
The markets closed the Friday afternoon kerb off highs at $1,183 and $7,800 respectively.
In aluminium, the market will be watching for a break from the $1,600-$1,650 price band which has walled in prices over the past few weeks.
Prices were probing under the $1,600 area on Monday morning.
A break above $1,650 would be significant, lifting the market above its long-term downtrend, Bahr said.
The market will eyeing the release of International Primary Aluminium Institute (IPAI) stocks data for December at 1100 GMT on Monday.
Total stocks to end November at Western world smelters fell to 3.090 million tonnes, compared with 3.161 million in October and 3.506 million in November 1995, provisional figures showed.
Unwrought metal stocks fell to 1.653 million tonnes versus 1.686 million and 1.930 million, respectively.
--Eric Onstad, London Newsroom +44 171 542-8065
